chapters.title: The Text — the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This course is all about Buddhist cosmology — all the different kinds of beings in the world. We're going to be studying a text called [CHOS MNGON PA MDZOD], the Abhidharmakosha — in shorthand, dzö [MDZOD], the last word here. So when you're talking to someone like Gibson — a super translator, an incredible scholar — and he asks, "what are you studying?" and you say, "dzö," he goes... you know, you're smart. It's called the Treasure House of Higher Knowledge.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It's the book about essentially all existing things — all existing things in the universe, mainly. And I say "mainly" because I have a scholar here who will argue with me; so if I just say "it's mainly about this," he can't argue with me. Primarily, it's about all existing things, from the point of view that I'm speaking from today. And this was written by Master Vasubandhu in 350 AD.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We started this class talking about why you're here. And now I'm taking a trip on this — let's talk about all existing things in the entire universe. You should be asking yourself a question: what is the relationship between understanding why you're here and studying all existing things? And specifically, we're talking about all the different types of beings that exist in the universe — the ones we can see with our eyes directly, and the ones we can't.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we're going to spend an entire week discussing all the different possibilities. Who are they? What do they look like? How do they live? What kind of life do they experience? What kind of birth do they have? What kind of death do they have? But more importantly, we're going to ask: what are the causes that create each of those types of beings? How would you become one?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, starting with the question — where was I before I was born? Where did I come from? In ACI Classics Course 4, we talked about past and future lives. I didn't forget which number, by the way — it's a teaching technique. It makes you feel like you're smarter than the teacher, right? If you're learning how to be a teacher, take note. Sometimes I honestly forget, and sometimes I pretend, and you'll never know the difference — except when I make a point of it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But seriously, the way we prove past and future lives is that we have to prove that everything is cause and effect. As things move forward toward your death, your mind at the time of death — does it just poof out of existence? A lot of belief systems — the word is drup-ta [GRUB MTHA'] — say that at the moment of death you poof out of existence, your mind just goes away. But after studying that course and understanding cause and effect, you see that the stuff of mind necessarily has to continue on.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We're not going to discuss the logic of it today, I'm sorry. But if you don't remember it, or you're new, ask somebody to explain it to you — talk to someone who does remember. The idea is that the stuff of mind, the material of mind, continues. Why? In a stream of cause and effect, an effect becomes a cause. Every cause has to have an effect; every cause has its own effect.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So does the chain of cause and effect ever stop? What would happen if it did? What's the logical conclusion you have to come to if the chain of cause and effect stops? There would be no cause and effect — you couldn't say there was ever any cause and effect, if effects stop.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I know it's been a couple of months — I've got to warm you up a bit, and I'm going quickly into a very deep topic. If cause and effect stopped, there wouldn't be any cause and effect at all. And you have to think about it. Again, I'm making your brains go. "I just want to be a bodhisattva and be compassionate." But it turns out that if you use your mind in a powerful way, it generates a kind of compassion that's unstoppable.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So if your mind is a series of causes and effects, this is how we prove future lives: because it has to continue on. Study the course and you'll understand why — I don't have time to prove it to you right now, and most of you went to the class. But what's the other conclusion? If it continues on, the seeds that you planted in this life have to continue on. They all have to ripen.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And what does that say about the first moment of this life? Did it just start from nothing? Did you just poof out of nothingness? Were you just not caused? If something uncaused just showed up, how could it create an effect? Nothing comes from nothing. There must have been a cause before.

chapters.title: Why This Life, and Not Another?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So — let's just pretend it's true. I didn't prove it to you, but pretend it's true for an hour. What causes were in play that created you right now? Why didn't you come out as a cat? Or a roach? Which roach? Good question — it depends what seed you have, to understand what I mean. Why do you have the seeds to even see a roach in your life? You have to start thinking that way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So in this course, we're going to study this: what came before that made you pop out as you — the uniqueness that you are? You are completely unique, different from every other human being on this planet. Your story, your life, all the things you've lived, are completely unique to you. So why me? In the good, the bad, and the ugly, as we say in English. And why not as a cat, or a hell being, or a form-realm being? We're going to explore all the different ways those beings are, but I want you to keep in mind what creates those beings in the first place.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then there's the infinite variety among us humans on this planet. There are lots of similarities, of course — regardless of race, we mostly all have two eyes, two arms, two legs, and a head. They might be different shapes and different colors. We might have different ideas about one thing or another. We might be accepting, or we might be racist about it. But all of those things and confluences together are what make you, you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then I'm going to ask a different question. If you continue on, and you make it all the way to 120 years old — or less — and then you have that final moment in this life, you should be asking yourself today: what's next? Am I guaranteed something cool afterward, or am I not? And what makes for that guarantee?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: You should be a little — we say in English — you should be pooping in your pants. You should be a little afraid, if you really think about it. What is going to guarantee that you're going to have something even this good? You don't realize how good you have it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: "But Tim, my life sucks. I have so much pain. My inner world is tumultuous. I have emotions. I don't have enough money. Things don't work out for me." That might be true. But if you shift your focus onto what brought you here, and how phenomenal this type of life is compared to others — the irony is that we don't really have direct memories of things that were better or worse. For the majority of life-types, according to Master Vasubandhu, this one is absolutely stellar and phenomenal compared to most of them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But we focus so much on the negative side of things. "This person excluded me." "They said something mean." I'll show you mean in about class four or five — and then you might feel a little differently about it. And it doesn't mean to diminish someone's pain — that's not what I'm saying. The pain is real. The pain can be intolerable at times. But there is some kind of great fortune that we have, being born as we are — even with the difficulties and challenges we all face, irrespective of what kind of family or what kind of place you're born into.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We're all in the same airplane — that's crashing. Sorry, depressing. We're all on the same airplane that's going down, called death. So the idea of this class is: what are we going to do while we're on the airplane? So that when that moment comes, we have a chance to throw the next life down into a better world than the one we already have.

chapters.title: The Commentary — Illumination of the Path to Freedom

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We're going to study a commentary by the first great teacher, Gendun Drup. It's called The Illumination of the Path to Freedom. He lived from 1391 to 1474.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right — let's start hitting the books, as we say in English. "Hitting the books" means "let's start studying." It doesn't mean actually hit the books.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, in the Buddhist understanding of the world, it's divided mainly into three places you can live — three categories: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Where are those realms? Where do they exist? We're going to ask this question.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I grew up a Christian. There's heaven, earth, and hell. Earth is here, heaven is up there, and hell is down there — you go up to heaven or down to hell depending on what kind of person you are, and you have one chance to live an eternal life in heaven, or an eternal life of damnation, suffering in hell forever. That's the belief system I come from.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I've been studying a lot of the differences between Eastern and Western thought. Western thought is very linear; Eastern philosophy is more cyclical. So it's interesting to compare the two, and how it plays out in Buddhism — because we kind of present both of them. And you have to think about why.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Anyhow, there are three realms — three categories of existence, three types of places. And each of those places is then divided into more. And we're not able to perceive all of them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The first one is called the desire realm — dö-kham ['DOD KHAMS]. Next is the form realm; there I see god-like beings — not God in a Judeo-Christian sense, but the highest element of form — and that's called suk-kam [GZUGS KHAMS]. And then the formless realm, suk-me-kam [GZUGS MED KHAMS] — kind of like empty space. We'll talk about that in a moment.
